directions: Plant container-grown divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring or early fall; Niveum epimedium is more compact and slower to spread than most barrenworts, so give it a protected spot where it will not be crowded out. This dainty hybrid barrenwort produces small, heart-shaped leaflets tinged bronze-red on emergence in spring, maturing to soft green, with airy sprays of small, pure white, spurred flowers held just above the foliage on wiry stems. Shear the previous year's tattered leaves to the ground in late winter before new growth and flowers emerge, since old foliage otherwise hides the bloom display. It is an excellent small-scale edger or front-of-border groundcover for dry shade under trees, tolerating root competition and summer drought once established better than most shade perennials.

directions: Plant container-grown divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring or early fall; Lilafee epimedium tolerates dry shade once established but establishes fastest with regular watering through its first season. New leaves emerge deep bronze-purple in early spring before greening for summer, and in the same flush the plant sends up wiry stems bearing showy, large, deep violet-purple, four-spurred flowers that hover like tiny orchids over the unfurling foliage — among the largest and darkest flowers of any commonly grown epimedium. Cut back old winter foliage to bare crowns in late winter just before new growth starts, since last year's leaves otherwise obscure the flower display. A superb choice for underplanting deciduous shrubs or lining a shaded path, it is deer- and rabbit-resistant and spreads slowly into a dense, weed-suppressing patch over several years.

planting.note: Plant dormant rhizome divisions in fall, or container-grown plants in spring, in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full to partial shade; this is a distinct species from the more common Polygonatum odoratum 'Variegatum' sold under a nearly identical name, with broader leaves and a stouter, more upright arch.

directions: Plant dormant rhizome divisions in fall, or container-grown plants in spring, in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full to partial shade; this is a distinct species from the more common Polygonatum odoratum 'Variegatum' sold under a nearly identical name, with broader leaves and a stouter, more upright arch. Gracefully arching stems carry broad, creamy-white-edged leaves in two ranks, with clusters of two to five small, tubular, greenish-white bells dangling from the leaf axils in late spring, followed by blue-black berries. Native to European woodlands, this variegated form of the classic Solomon's seal brings strong vertical structure and season-long brightness to a shaded border, combining well with hostas, ferns, and hellebores. Top-dress annually with compost or leaf mold and keep soil from drying out in summer; established clumps need dividing only every five to seven years.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

common_name: Albostriata Lily of the Valley (Striped-Leaf Lily of the Valley)

planting.note: Plant dormant pips (rhizome divisions) in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Albostriata spreads by rhizome as vigorously as the plain species, so confine it with a buried barrier or edging where a contained planting is wanted.

directions: Plant dormant pips (rhizome divisions) in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Albostriata spreads by rhizome as vigorously as the plain species, so confine it with a buried barrier or edging where a contained planting is wanted. Each broad, glossy leaf is finely pin-striped in creamy white from base to tip, a variegation that holds well through the season and reads as a shimmer of light across a shaded bed even before the classic sprays of small, nodding, intensely fragrant white bells open in mid-spring. It naturalizes readily into a dense, weed-smothering carpet in the deep, dry shade under trees where few flowering groundcovers thrive, but every part of the plant, including the small red berries, is toxic if ingested, so site it away from children's play areas or vegetable beds. Division is rarely needed and mainly done to control spread or share pips.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Start transplants or plant container-grown divisions in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Tara prairie dropseed is slow to establish in its first year or two before its extensive root system takes hold, so keep young plantings weeded and watered.

directions: Start transplants or plant container-grown divisions in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Tara prairie dropseed is slow to establish in its first year or two before its extensive root system takes hold, so keep young plantings weeded and watered. Bred at Iowa State University for a more uniform, compact habit than the wild species, this selection forms a neat, fine-textured fountain of glossy, hair-thin green leaves that turns bright orange to copper in fall, with airy seed panicles in late summer that release a distinctive fragrance often compared to popcorn or coriander. It holds its shape through winter and needs no staking or division, making it one of the lowest-maintenance native grasses for a formal border edge, mass planting, or prairie-style garden. Cut the whole clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth resumes each spring.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

planting.note: Start transplants indoors or direct sow in spring in lean, gravelly to sandy, very well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; silky-spike melic thrives on poor, dry soils and develops floppy, weak growth if the soil is too rich or moist.

directions: Start transplants indoors or direct sow in spring in lean, gravelly to sandy, very well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; silky-spike melic thrives on poor, dry soils and develops floppy, weak growth if the soil is too rich or moist. Narrow, blue-green foliage forms a tidy clump topped in early summer by dense, cylindrical, silvery-white flower spikes covered in silky hairs that catch the light and sway with the slightest breeze, aging to a soft buff tan that persists into fall. Native to dry, rocky, calcareous slopes across central and southern Europe, it is a well-mannered, non-spreading clumper ideal for a gravel garden, rock garden, or dry border where taller grasses would overwhelm smaller companions. Cut the previous season's foliage back hard in late winter before new growth begins.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; false lily of the valley spreads slowly and politely by rhizome, unlike the aggressive true lily of the valley it resembles.

directions: Plant container-grown divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; false lily of the valley spreads slowly and politely by rhizome, unlike the aggressive true lily of the valley it resembles. Glossy, evergreen, strap-shaped leaves form a low, tidy rosette from which short spikes of small, star-shaped, fragrant white flowers rise in mid-spring, giving it a passing resemblance to lily of the valley without that plant's toxicity concerns or runaway spread. Native to moist woodland understories in central China, it holds its foliage year-round in mild climates, making it a useful evergreen edger or small-scale groundcover under shrubs and trees where a well-behaved companion to hellebores and hostas is wanted. It resents hot, dry conditions, so keep soil consistently moist and mulch to conserve moisture through summer.
